cards.back: Standard call-level **APIs** for embedding DB access in app programs (Java=JDBC, generic=ODBC). Python uses a DB-API driver (`mysql.connector`).
**connect → cursor → execute → commit/rollback → fetch → close.** Use **parameterised queries** (`%s`) to prevent SQL injection.
Smallest unit of work — a set of read/write operations that **all happen or none happen** (all-or-nothing). Ends with COMMIT or ROLLBACK.
**Atomicity** (all-or-none), **Consistency** (valid→valid state), **Isolation** (appear to run alone), **Durability** (committed changes persist after crash).
**A & D** → recovery system (via the **log**, undo/redo). **I** → concurrency-control system. **C** → atomicity + isolation + app correctness.
**read(X)** copies item X from disk into a buffer variable. **write(X)** copies the variable back to X (often buffered, flushed later). Buffer eviction: **LRU**.
**active → partially committed → committed**; or **active → failed → aborted → terminated**. Commit point = entering committed (durability kicks in).
Sequential disk file recording each write's **old & new values** + start/commit/abort. Recovery uses it to **undo** uncommitted and **redo** committed transactions.
**Recoverable**: commit only after read-from txns commit. **Cascadeless**: read only committed data (no cascading aborts). **Strict**: read/write only after last writer committed (simplest recovery).
**Lost update** (write overwritten), **Dirty read** (read uncommitted, later rolled back), **Incorrect summary** (aggregate over mid-update data), **Unrepeatable read** (two reads differ).
**Dirty read** = reads *uncommitted* data that may roll back. **Unrepeatable read** = reads *committed* data that another txn changes between two reads.
**Improved throughput & resource utilisation** (CPU works while another txn waits on I/O) and **reduced waiting time** — worth the cost of concurrency control.
**READ UNCOMMITTED** (dirty,nonrep,phantom) → **READ COMMITTED** (nonrep,phantom) → **REPEATABLE READ** (phantom) → **SERIALIZABLE** (none). SERIALIZABLE = strongest & SQL default.
A **newly INSERTED row** (matching a WHERE condition) that appears in a re-run range query. Distinct from non-repeatable read (a changed value). Only SERIALIZABLE prevents it.
**Dirty read** (uncommitted), **Non-repeatable read** (changed value on re-read), **Phantom** (inserted row in range query).
**Different transactions + same item + at least one write.** So R-W, W-R, W-W conflict. R-R, different items, and same-transaction ops never conflict.
**Serial** = no interleaving (one txn at a time). **Serializable** = interleaved but equivalent to *some* serial schedule → consistent, with concurrency.
A schedule transformable into a serial one by **swapping adjacent NON-conflicting operations**. (Swapping non-conflicting ops never changes the result.)
Node per txn; edge **Ti→Tj** if a conflicting op of Tj follows Ti's on the same item (W-R/R-W/W-W). **Acyclic ⇒ conflict serializable.**
**Cycle ⇒ NOT conflict serializable.** Acyclic ⇒ serializable; **topological sort** (repeatedly remove in-degree-0 node) gives the equivalent serial order.

cards.front: Why not test serializability at runtime?
cards.back: It needs the whole schedule after the fact. Instead a **protocol** (2PL) guarantees only serializable schedules are produced. The graph proves protocols & solves problems.
Same **initial reads** + same **read-from** relationships + same **final writes** (last writer of each item). View serializable = view-equivalent to a serial schedule.
**Serial ⊂ Conflict-serializable ⊂ View-serializable ⊂ All.** Every conflict-SR is view-SR, not vice-versa.
A **write with no prior read** of that item by the same transaction. Blind writes make some schedules view-serializable but NOT conflict-serializable.

cards.front: Why prefer conflict over view SR?
cards.back: Conflict SR is a cheap **precedence-graph cycle check**; view SR testing is **NP-complete**. Protocols enforce the easier conflict serializability.
**S** = read only, many holders. **X** = read+write, one holder. Compatibility: **only S–S is compatible**; anything with X conflicts.
Two+ txns each wait for a lock the other holds → none progress. Resolve by **rolling back** a victim (MySQL auto-detects via wait-for graph).
A txn waiting for an X-lock is repeatedly overtaken by S-lock grants → never proceeds. Fixed by **FIFO** lock granting (lock table).
Releasing a lock **too early** breaks serializability (another txn reads an inconsistent intermediate state). The fix: **two-phase locking**.
**Growing**: acquire locks, release none. **Shrinking**: release locks, acquire none. After the first release no new locks. **Lock point** = end of growing phase.
**Guarantees conflict serializability** (serialize in lock-point order) but **NOT deadlock-freedom**. Deadlock handled separately.
**Strict**: hold all **X**-locks till commit/abort (recoverable, no cascade). **Rigorous**: hold **all** locks till commit (serialize by commit order). Most DBs use rigorous.
**Growing**: upgrade S→X (need more access). **Shrinking**: downgrade X→S. Upgrades only while growing, downgrades only while shrinking.
**Not Only SQL** — non-tabular, **schema-less** DBs for big/unstructured data; emphasise scalability, availability, replication over strong consistency & rich queries.
**Document** (MongoDB), **Key-value** (Redis, DynamoDB), **Wide-column** (Cassandra, HBase), **Graph** (Neo4j).

Can't guarantee all three: **C**onsistency, **A**vailability, **P**artition-tolerance — pick **2**. Since partitions are unavoidable, the real choice is **C vs A**. NoSQL → **A+P** (eventual consistency).
**CAP consistency** = all replicas agree on the value. **ACID consistency** = a transaction preserves integrity constraints. Same word, different concepts.
**Replication**: copy data across nodes (master-slave / master-master) for availability. **Sharding**: partition records across nodes for load balancing.
Open-source **in-memory key-value** store (RAM + disk persistence). Schema-less, very fast; Lua scripting, master-slave replication. `:` denotes key namespacing.
**String**, **List** (linked list), **Hash** (field-value map), **Set** (unique unordered), **Sorted Set/Zset** (members with scores, sorted).
Members each have a **score**; kept sorted by score (ties → lexicographic). The structure for **leaderboards**. `ZADD`, `ZRANGE`, `ZREVRANGE`, `ZRANK`.
**EXPIRE** key sec (auto-delete after timeout), **TTL** (remaining time), **PERSIST** (remove timeout), **DEL** (delete now). Used for caching/sessions.
RAM **expensive**, **manual** eviction config, **data loss** risk on crash (in-memory), **not for complex joins/aggregations** (key-lookup optimised).
**Nodes** (entities, with ≥0 **labels**) + **directed relationships** (with a **type**) + **properties** (key-value, on nodes AND relationships) + **paths**.
**Efficient handling of highly connected data** — fast traversals via direct relationship pointers vs costly relational JOINs. Used for social nets, recommendations, fraud.
Neo4j's declarative query language. `CREATE (n:Label {prop:val})`, `CREATE (a)-[:TYPE]->(b)`, `MATCH (a)-[:TYPE]->(b) RETURN ...`. `→` = relationship direction.
Neo4j relationships are **directed** & a node may have **no label**; ER relationships undirected & every entity has a type. Neo4j = real DBMS; ER = design tool.
Stores high-dimensional **vectors**, retrieves by **similarity (semantic meaning)** not exact match. For ML embeddings, recommendations, semantic search, **RAG**.
A vector from an **embedding model** (OpenAI, Google) capturing the **semantic meaning** of text/image/audio — similar objects map to nearby vectors ('doctor' ≈ 'physician').
**Cosine similarity** (cos θ: 1=very similar, 0=unrelated, −1=opposite) and **Euclidean distance**. Cosine is standard for text.
**KNN** (exact), **ANN** (approximate, for big data), **HNSW** (hierarchical graph, fast+memory-efficient), **IVFPQ** (inverted file + product quantization).
**FTS**: words/stems, inverted index, TF-IDF/BM25 ranking, text only. **Vector search**: meaning, vector index (HNSW), distance ranking, handles synonyms + any modality.
PostgreSQL extension: `CREATE EXTENSION vector;` adds a `VECTOR(n)` type; `CREATE INDEX ... USING hnsw (embedding vector_cosine_ops)` for semantic similarity search.
Before a write, the log records the **old value**. On failure: **undo** uncommitted txns from the log; **redo** committed ones whose writes didn't reach disk. Gives **atomicity + durability**.
In-memory structure the **lock manager** keeps: a list per item of granted/waiting requests + modes. FIFO granting guarantees **freedom from starvation**.
Two schedules with the same final state are **result equivalent** — but this may be **accidental** (only for specific values), so it can't define equivalence. Use conflict/view equivalence.
